channels.name: Hacker News (Show HN)
channels.title: Show HN: GitAnalytics – Local-first git visualizer because cloud audits are painful
channels.instructions: Post as a "Show HN" link. Use the link to your free GitHub OSS repository. Paste the comment below as the initial text instantly after posting.
channels.postBody:
Hi HN,

I built GitAnalytics (https://github.com/raycoding1-collab/git-analytics-oss) because I got tired of cloud analytics tools asking for full write-permissions to my private GitHub repositories just to display a few basic charts.

It runs locally as a zero-dependency CLI tool (uses pure Node.js built-ins) and generates a single self-contained HTML report. The HTML has all the logic, styling, and charts embedded, meaning you can double-click it and inspect the data fully offline.

Key engineering challenges:
- **No dependencies**: Written using pure `child_process`, `fs`, and `path` built-ins. Node's standard executable is all that is required.
- **Handling massive repositories**: When running `git log --numstat` on codebases with 50,000+ commits, standard node buffers overflow and crash. I resolved this by configuring safe maximum memory thresholds (100MB) and strict error handling.
- **Timezone/OS alignment**: Used strict ISO 8601 formatting flags on the git logs (`%aI`) so that JavaScript parses the commit dates identically across different Windows, macOS, and Linux system locales.

The repository is open-sourced under the MIT license. I'd love to get feedback on the parsing efficiency, or what other metrics you'd find useful in a local codebase report.

channels.name: Reddit (r/SideProject)
channels.title: I got tired of cloud analytics demanding access to my private repos, so I built a zero-dependency local git visualizer.
channels.instructions: Post as a Link post in r/SideProject (or r/selfhosted). Link to the free GitHub OSS repository. Paste this text as the post description or initial comment.
channels.postBody:
Hey guys,

A few weeks ago, I wanted to review my team's sprint velocity and get a breakdown of lines of code growth over the last quarter. Every visualizer I found online wanted me to log in with GitHub and grant read/write access to my private organization repos.

For client work and IP compliance, that's a absolute dealbreaker.

So I built a small tool called GitAnalytics (https://github.com/raycoding1-collab/git-analytics-oss). It runs entirely locally on your machine via a single CLI execution:

`npx git-analytics-oss`

It parses the git log history, base64 encodes it, and injects it into a gorgeous interactive HTML report that opens in your browser. 
- **Zero dependencies**: No packages to install, just runs on standard Node.js.
- **100% offline**: Once the HTML file is generated, you can open it on an airplane or email it directly to clients.
- **Secure**: No servers, no APIs, no tracking.

The code is fully open-source. I'd love to hear your thoughts or see if you run into any parsing bugs on massive repos (I tested it on big repositories, and it handled them without buffer crashes). Let me know what you think!

channels.name: Indie Hackers
channels.title: Case Study: Using an open-source Trojan Horse to sell a paid developer tool
channels.instructions: Post as a Text Post in the "Products" or "Marketing" groups on Indie Hackers. Link to your GitHub OSS repository as the project.
channels.postBody:
Hey IH community,

I've been experimenting with building micro-products for developers, and I wanted to share the launch strategy I'm using for GitAnalytics Pro ($12 paid dashboard).

Instead of trying to run ads or do outbound sales (which developers hate), I'm launching an "Open Core" Trojan Horse strategy:

1. **The Free Hook**: I released a clean, MIT-licensed open-source tool on GitHub (https://github.com/raycoding1-collab/git-analytics-oss) that generates basic git log charts locally.
2. **The Perceived Value**: Inside the free HTML report and the repo README, I include a feature comparison table comparing it to the Pro version (which adds conventional commits summaries, work rhythm radar charts, and refactoring hotspot analysis).
3. **The Upgrades**: The Pro version is sold via Gumroad for a one-time fee of $12 (no SaaS subscriptions).

This does two things:
- It gets developers sharing a cool, free open-source tool on Hacker News and Reddit without it feeling like spam.
- The repository acts as an organic SEO landing page that continuously funnels high-intent buyers to the Gumroad page.

I'd love to hear if anyone else has run this open-core loop for developer utilities, and I'll keep you posted on the conversion rates in a follow-up post!
